title: Report Writing: The Official (Incident) Report
summary: The features of a formal report (formal tone, past tense, passive voice) and the format of an incident report with a model.

p: A report is a formal, structured document that presents facts about an event, situation or investigation. Its main purpose is to inform, not to entertain or give personal opinion. Objectivity and clarity matter most.

Formal tone: use standard English, no contractions (do not, not don't) and no slang. Past tense: a report describes things that have already happened. Passive voice: often used to stress the action rather than the doer, which makes the report more objective. Active: The student broke the window. Passive: The window was broken.

Title: clear and descriptive, such as REPORT ON THE VANDALISM OF SCHOOL PROPERTY. To: the reader (The Principal). From: your name and position (John Bako, Senior Prefect). Date: the date of submission.
Introduction: the purpose, what happened, where and when. Example: This report describes the vandalism that took place in the SS3 Science Laboratory on the evening of Monday, 12th November, 2025.

Body (findings): a chronological, factual account in paragraphs. Example: At about 4:15 p.m. I was alerted by a noise from the laboratory. On investigation, I found that three glass beakers had been broken. The laboratory attendant, Mr. Musa, was called and the scene was secured.

Conclusion and recommendation: the outcome and next steps. Example: In conclusion, property worth about ₦25,000 was destroyed. It is recommended that the school management review security after hours and that the culprits, if identified, be made to replace the damaged items.
Sign-off: signature and full name.

Give times, places and names. Report only what you saw or what you were told, and say which is which. Do not add opinions. Use the passive voice where it helps, but do not use it so much that the report is hard to read.

title: Report of a Meeting: Minutes
summary: How to write the minutes of a meeting: title, attendance, apologies, agenda, matters arising, business, any other business and adjournment.

p: Minutes are the official report of a meeting. They record who attended, what was discussed, what was decided and who is to do what. They are written in the past tense, in a formal and objective tone.
Title: MINUTES OF THE MEETING OF THE LITERARY AND DEBATING SOCIETY HELD ON (date) AT (place).
Present: the list of people who attended. Absent with apology: those who told the secretary beforehand that they could not come.
Agenda: the list of topics.
1. Opening: the time and any formalities such as the opening prayer.
2. Matters arising: reading and approving the minutes of the last meeting, and follow-up on actions from it.
3. Business of the day: an account of each item on the agenda, with the discussion, the decisions and who is responsible for each action. An Action column may help.
4. Any other business (A.O.B.): topics not on the main agenda.
5. Adjournment: the time the meeting ended.
Signatures: the secretary and the chairman or president.

The body of an incident report is a chronological account of what happened. The business of the day in minutes is organised by agenda item, not by time, and records decisions and responsibilities. Both use formal language and the past tense.

The meeting was called to order at 2:00 p.m. by the President, Miss Amaka Obi, who led the opening prayer. The minutes of the last meeting were read, corrected and adopted. Under business of the day, the Secretary reported that the society's debate against Government College would hold on 3rd March. It was resolved that five members would represent the society. Mr. Eze was asked to prepare the team. There being no other business, the meeting was adjourned at 3:15 p.m.

activity: Write the minutes of a class meeting (invent names and dates) that discussed a class excursion. Include present, absent with apology, agenda, matters arising, business, A.O.B. and adjournment.

title: Comprehension: Corruption
summary: A comprehension passage on corruption with five questions of different types and model answers.

p: Corruption is a cancer that has metastasized to every part of our nation's body politic. It is not just the politician who embezzles public funds; it is the clerk who demands a 'softener' to find your file, the student who pays to have exam questions leaked, and the citizen who offers a 'tip' to a police officer to avoid a penalty. This endemic culture of 'cutting corners' has dire consequences.

Firstly, it destroys meritocracy. When jobs and contracts are awarded because of nepotism or bribes rather than skill and qualification, the most competent people are pushed aside. This leads to profound inefficiency: bridges collapse because the contractor used substandard materials, and public services fail because the managers are incompetent. Secondly, it creates a deep public cynicism. Citizens begin to believe that success is impossible through hard work and honesty, leading to a breakdown of societal values and an increase in petty and grand corruption.

1. (Factual) Besides politicians, what two other examples of corrupt acts are given? Answer: A clerk who demands a softener (a bribe) to find a file, a student who pays to have exam questions leaked, and a citizen who gives a tip to a police officer to avoid a penalty. Any two.

2. (Vocabulary) What does 'metastasized' suggest about corruption? Answer: It suggests that corruption has spread from one place to every part of society, as a cancer spreads through the body, and is dangerous and hard to remove.
3. (Vocabulary) The meaning of 'nepotism'. Answer: Favouring relatives or friends, for example by giving them jobs, without regard to merit.

4. (Inferential) The first major consequence and its direct result. Answer: Corruption destroys meritocracy (the system of rewarding ability); the direct result is profound inefficiency because the most competent people are sidelined.

5. (Global) The author's main argument about citizens' attitudes. Answer: Corruption makes citizens cynical; they come to believe that hard work and honesty cannot bring success, so values break down and corruption increases.

Unqualified people get contracts and jobs. A contractor who got a contract through bribes uses poor materials, so bridges collapse. Managers who got their posts through nepotism are incompetent, so public services fail.

title: Vocabulary: Idioms and Idiomatic Expressions
summary: Six common idioms with meanings and examples, and how to use idioms in your own writing.

p: Idioms are fixed expressions whose meanings are not clear from the words themselves. They are an important part of fluent, natural English and are often tested in comprehension and essays.
Born with a silver spoon in one's mouth: to be born into a rich and privileged family. Example: He never worried about tuition fees; he was born with a silver spoon in his mouth.

The black sheep of the family: a person whom the family sees as a disgrace or failure, often because he is different or has done something shameful. Example: While all his brothers are doctors and lawyers, Ade is the black sheep of the family for becoming an artist.

Take the bull by the horns: to face a difficult or dangerous situation directly and bravely. Example: Instead of ignoring the debts, the manager took the bull by the horns and reorganised the company's finances.
Spill the beans: to reveal a secret, often by accident. Example: We were planning a surprise party, but her brother spilled the beans a day before.
Once in a blue moon: very rarely. Example: He visits his hometown once in a blue moon.

A chip on one's shoulder: an attitude of constant hostility or defensiveness because of a feeling of having been wronged or of being inferior. Example: He has had a chip on his shoulder ever since he was passed over for promotion.

Use an idiom only when it fits the meaning. Do not change the words: say take the bull by the horns, not take the cow by the horns. Do not use too many in one piece of writing. In formal essays use idioms sparingly. In the examination, if you are asked for the meaning of an idiom, give the figurative meaning, not the literal one.

title: Listening: Following Instructions Accurately
summary: Strategies for following spoken instructions: signal words, prepositions, visualising and checking, with a practice example.

p: Following instructions correctly is vital in school, at work and in daily life. It needs active, focused listening and careful processing.
a. Remove distractions and listen actively. Do not assume you know what comes next.
b. Notice signal words. Sequence: first, then, next, after that, finally. Condition: before you begin, once you have, if... then... Priority: the most important step is, make sure that, crucially.
c. Notice small prepositions that change meaning: in the box and on the box; through the door and towards the door.
d. Visualise the process: make a mental film of yourself doing the steps.
e. Confirm and clarify: repeat the instructions in your own words or ask a precise question, such as So, after I connect the red wire, should I turn the switch on or off?

Instruction: To assemble this bookshelf, first lay the side panels on the floor. Then, using the longer screws, attach the back panel to the side panels. Before you tighten them completely, slot in the middle shelves. Finally, tighten all the screws fully and turn the bookshelf upright.

Analysis: the sequence words (first, then, finally) and the condition (before you tighten them completely) are vital. If you tighten the screws before slotting in the shelves, the shelves will not fit.
Make a list: 1. Lay the side panels on the floor. 2. Attach the back panel with the longer screws. 3. Slot in the middle shelves. 4. Tighten all the screws. 5. Stand the bookshelf upright.

In the examination, the instructions on the paper are the first test of this skill. Read them carefully: 'in one sentence', 'list two', 'not more than 50 words' and 'answer any three questions' all change what you must do.

title: Reading: Summarising Argumentative Passages
summary: How to find the thesis, supporting reasons, counter-argument and rebuttal in an argumentative passage, and how to write a short summary from them.

p: Summarising an argument means finding not only what the author says but how the case is built.

a. Find the core argument (thesis): the one sentence that shows the author's stand, in the introduction or conclusion. Example: The government should introduce a sugar tax to combat rising obesity and diabetes.

b. Find the supporting reasons (pillars): usually one in each body paragraph. Pillar 1: A sugar tax would reduce the consumption of sugary drinks. Pillar 2: The money raised could pay for public health campaigns.

c. Find the counter-argument and rebuttal, if present. A strong argument admits the opposing view and then answers it. Counter-argument: Critics say a sugar tax is regressive and unfairly hits the poor. Rebuttal: However, the health benefits for poorer communities, who suffer most from these diseases, would far outweigh the small financial cost.
d. Write the summary: join these elements in a short paragraph.

The author argues for a sugar tax to improve public health, saying it would reduce consumption and pay for health programmes. Although he admits that the tax may be regressive, he maintains that the health benefits for vulnerable groups justify it.
argues, claims, maintains, contends, admits, acknowledges, concedes, rejects, refutes, concludes.

title: Grammar: Adverbial Clauses
summary: Adverbial clauses of cause, purpose, condition and contrast, with signal words, examples and practice.

p: An adverbial clause is a subordinate clause that works as an adverb. It modifies a verb, an adjective or another adverb and gives information about time, reason, condition and so on. It cannot stand alone as a sentence.
Cause or reason (Why?): because, since, as. The match was cancelled because the pitch was waterlogged.
Purpose (For what aim?): so that, in order that. He saved his money so that he could buy a new laptop.
Condition (Under what condition?): if, unless, provided that, as long as. If it rains tomorrow, the outdoor concert will be moved indoors. You will not succeed unless you work hard.

Contrast or concession (In spite of what?): although, though, even though, while, whereas. Although he was the favourite, he lost the election. I prefer romantic comedies, while my brother prefers action films.
(Adverbial clauses of time use when, before, after, until, while. Clauses of place use where and wherever.)

Do not use two conjunctions together: Although he was very rich, he was not happy (not Although he was very rich but he was not happy). Use a comma after an adverbial clause that comes first. Unless means if not: do not write unless you do not work.

I will not speak to him again unless he apologises (condition). She left the house early so that she would not miss the bus (purpose). Although he was injured, he managed to finish the race (contrast). The students were excited because the trip had been confirmed (cause).
In 'She studied every day so that she would pass her exams', the adverbial clause is so that she would pass her exams: a clause of purpose.

title: Report Writing: The Investigative Report
summary: The template of a formal investigative report: terms of reference, procedure, findings, conclusion and recommendations, with a model on missing sports equipment.

p: An investigative report is a formal document that presents the findings of an inquiry. It must be objective and based on evidence, and it must lead the reader logically from the question to the conclusion.
Title: REPORT OF THE INVESTIGATION INTO THE THEFT OF SPORTS EQUIPMENT. To: The Principal. From: your name, Chairman, Students' Disciplinary Committee. Date.

1.0 Introduction (terms of reference): why the investigation was held and what it was to find out. Example: This report presents the findings of the investigation begun on 18th May, 2025, on the instruction of the Principal, into the disappearance of footballs and jerseys from the sports store.

2.0 Procedure: how the investigation was done. Example: The committee examined the store's inventory and sign-out log and interviewed the Sports Prefect, the storekeeper and three members of the football team.

3.0 Findings: a neutral presentation of the evidence, in numbered points. 3.1 The inventory check showed a shortage of five footballs and ten jerseys. 3.2 The sign-out log for the past month was incomplete. 3.3 The Sports Prefect stated that he had lent the equipment to a community youth team without permission. 3.4 The storekeeper confirmed this and said he had been pressed to release the items.

4.0 Conclusion: a short summary of the facts established. The committee concludes that the missing equipment was taken from the store by the Sports Prefect, who lent it to an unauthorised outside group against school policy.

5.0 Recommendations: practical suggestions based on the conclusion. The committee recommends that: (i) the Sports Prefect be relieved of his duties; (ii) the missing equipment be recovered at once; (iii) a stricter system for checking out sports equipment be introduced.
Sign-off: signature, name and position.
Findings are the facts and evidence discovered, set out neutrally in detail. The conclusion is a short statement of what those facts prove. Recommendations say what should be done about it.

title: Drama: Listening to Plays and the Architecture of a Play
summary: How to listen for meaning in a dramatic performance, and the terms act, scene, dialogue, monologue, soliloquy, aside, stage directions, plot, climax and theme.

p: When you listen to a radio play or a performance, you are an aural detective. There is no picture, so every sound is a clue.

Tone of voice and delivery: a character's true feelings are often shown by how something is said: trembling with fear, booming with authority, sneering, hesitant. Pace, pitch and volume carry subtext.
Sound effects: rain and thunder set a scene of trouble; a door slamming shows an argument; approaching footsteps build suspense.
Music and silence: music sets the mood (tense, romantic, tragic). Silence can be stronger than words, showing shock or deep thought.

Plot is the chain of events. Find the central conflict: man against man (two characters opposed), man against society (a character challenging traditions or laws) or man against himself (inner doubt). Theme is the central idea the play explores: the corrupting effect of power, the struggle between tradition and change, the strength of love.
Act: a major division of a play, like a chapter. Scene: a part of an act, usually a change of place or a jump in time.

Dialogue: conversation between characters, the main way of telling the story. Monologue: a long speech by one character to others who are on stage. Soliloquy: a speech by a character alone on stage, speaking his private thoughts aloud to the audience; Hamlet's To be, or not to be is a soliloquy. Aside: a short remark spoken to the audience that the other characters on stage, by convention, cannot hear.

Stage directions are the bracketed or italic words in a script that are not spoken. They describe the setting, movements, expressions, tones and sound effects. Example: [KOLA enters abruptly, slamming the door. He is breathing heavily and looks frantic.]
Climax: the highest point of tension, or the turning point of the plot, where the main conflict must be faced and resolved.

title: Revision of a Prescribed Text: The Blood of a Stranger
summary: The plot, characters and themes of Dele Charley's play The Blood of a Stranger, with corrections to common mistakes about the story.

p: The Blood of a Stranger is a play by the Sierra Leonean playwright Dele Charley. (Some printed notes give the author as D.K. Gbegba; the author is Dele Charley.) It is set in the traditional kingdom of Mandoland and is a symbolic story of colonial exploitation.
Check this text against your own copy of the play and your teacher's notes, because published summaries differ in small details.

Maligu, the king's literate chief adviser, persuades the priest Soko to invent a prophecy that a stranger is coming. King Santigi and the people accept it; only Kindo, the chief warrior and heir to the throne, doubts it. Mr. Whitehead, a white colonial agent, arrives and says that he wants to farm tobacco, but he really wants the land's diamonds. He refuses to pay homage to the king and gives the villagers liquor, and the community begins to break down. His Black assistant, Parker, does his dirty work.

Soko, afraid, wants to withdraw from the scheme, and Whitehead has him killed by Parker. Kindo then kills Parker. A false sacrifice is staged, in which Maligu plays the priest and Parker's blood is spilled instead of that of a maiden. Kindo exposes the plot, but Maligu and Whitehead have him banished and the king agrees. At the end, Whitehead dies at Kindo's spear and Kindo goes into exile.

Whitehead: a colonial agent, greedy and dishonest; his name is symbolic. Maligu: the greedy, literate adviser who betrays his people for money. Kindo: the brave and honest warrior, the only one who sees the truth. Soko: the priest who is forced to lie and pays with his life. Santigi: the weak and easily led king. Wara: Kindo's woman, treated as an outsider because of her mother's background; she resists Whitehead. Parker: Whitehead's assistant.

Colonial exploitation: Whitehead is a symbol of colonial powers that came to Africa under false pretences to take its wealth. Greed and betrayal: Maligu and Soko betray the community for personal gain. Tradition and its misuse: the priest's authority is used for selfish ends. Integrity: Kindo alone questions the lies. Outsiders: Wara is a stranger in her own community.
Types of conflict: man against man (Kindo against Whitehead and Maligu), man against society (Kindo against the king and a deceived people).

sections.h: A note on what the earlier notes got wrong
p: Some textbooks say that Kindo is killed, that Soko is exiled and that the villagers rise up under Wara to kill Whitehead. In the play, Kindo is banished, Soko is killed on Whitehead's order, and Whitehead dies at Kindo's spear. Always use the text itself in an examination.

title: Second Term Revision and Practice Assignment
summary: A revision checklist of every topic of Second Term and a full practice assignment with model answers.

p: Vocabulary: government and administration (democracy, revenue, bureaucracy, agency, white paper, gazette, circular, memorandum, agenda, minutes, Permanent Secretary, cadre); law and order (plaintiff, defendant, tribunal, justice, civil rights, litigation, verdict, acquitted, convicted); idioms (six); Latin and Greek roots.
Spoken English and listening: rhythm, rhyme, tone and enjambment; paraphrasing a poem heard; logos, pathos, ethos and rebuttal; following instructions; listening to drama.
Grammar: adjuncts (time, place, manner, reason, frequency); defining and non-defining clauses; adverbial clauses (cause, purpose, condition, contrast); simple, compound and complex sentences.
Writing: audience and register; revising an expository essay; letter to the editor; incident report; minutes; investigative report.
Reading: summary by outlining; summarising an argument; paraphrasing; comprehension.
Literature (drama): act, scene, dialogue, monologue, soliloquy, aside, stage directions, plot, climax, theme; The Blood of a Stranger.

1. Correct the errors. (a) The man who his car was stolen reported to the police. (b) Although he was very rich but he was not happy. (c) The principal, gave the students, who failed, a stern warning.

Model answers: (a) The man whose car was stolen reported to the police. (b) Although he was very rich, he was not happy. (c) The principal gave the students who failed a stern warning. (If only some students failed and the clause is extra information, the clause may be set off by commas: The principal gave the students, who had failed, a stern warning. In (c) the original comma after principal is wrong in either case.)

2. Vocabulary. (a) The government will soon publish a white paper on its findings. (b) The lawyer argued that his client's civil rights had been violated. (c) He was born with a silver spoon and never had to work.
3. Writing. Write a letter of not more than 150 words to the editor, for or against: Mobile phones should be banned in secondary schools. Use a title and the correct format.

4. Summary. In three sentences, summarise the two main consequences of corruption and the underlying cause in the Week 8 passage. Model: Corruption destroys meritocracy because jobs and contracts go to relatives and bribes instead of to the qualified, which leads to inefficiency such as collapsing bridges and failing services. It also makes citizens cynical, so that they believe hard work and honesty cannot succeed, and values break down. The underlying cause is a widespread culture of cutting corners, in which many people offer or accept bribes.
